overview: Founded in 1918, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes became Yugoslavia in 1929. After wartime partition and conflict, a six-republic socialist federation emerged in 1945.

periods.title: A kingdom with competing visions
periods.summary: The monarchy united diverse territories, then adopted the name Yugoslavia under a royal dictatorship in 1929.

periods.title: Occupation and war
periods.summary: Axis powers invaded and partitioned the country. Occupation, mass persecution and fighting between resistance movements devastated communities.

periods.title: The socialist federation
periods.summary: Tito’s federation broke with Stalin in 1948, developed its own socialist system and repressed political opposition.

periods.title: Dissolution and war
periods.summary: Republics separated in 1991 and 1992 as the federation collapsed amid conflict.

items.text: Rapid urban growth created a serious need for housing after the Second World War. Architects used prefabricated construction to build on a large scale. The resulting apartments were also experiments in arranging limited space for ordinary activities such as sleeping, eating and family gatherings.

Yugoslav apartment designs could include rooms with several uses, flexible layouts and balconies extending living space outdoors. Architects compared ideas through competitions and published plans. A modest flat still required careful thought about where people would cook, work, rest and spend time together.

The 1963 earthquake devastated Skopje, in the Yugoslav republic of Macedonia. Its reconstruction brought together local and international planners, including Japanese architect Kenzo Tange. New buildings and city plans emerged through this collaboration, making rebuilding both an urgent practical task and an architectural experiment.

Davorin Savnik designed the ETA 80 telephone for Iskra in 1979. Its unusually flat, clean shape attracted attention in industrial design. The Museum of Architecture and Design preserves the model, a reminder that an object used for an ordinary phone call could also be carefully designed.

Niko Kralj’s folding Rex lounge chair dates to 1956. Cuts in its plywood help the wood curve into the seat and back, while the whole chair folds away. It solves two domestic problems at once: somewhere comfortable to sit and somewhere to put the chair afterward.

Branko Ćopić’s children’s story first appeared as Ježeva kuća in 1949, illustrated by Aljoša Josić. The museum catalogue records a print run of five thousand and an Italian translation in 1951. A story associated with generations of childhood reading could travel across languages quite quickly.

sections.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories

items.text: Youth work actions combined organized labor with group life. The Museum of Yugoslavia describes competitions between brigades in work, sport and cultural activities, as well as shared songs and greetings. Their surviving objects and memories connect construction projects with the experiences of young participants.

Workers’ self-management became a central idea in Yugoslav socialism. The constitutional law of 1953 assigned management rights to workers and producers. These legal arrangements aimed to give workplaces a role in running enterprises, within a system that still had Communist political leadership.

Belgrade hosted the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. Yugoslavia sought international relationships beyond membership in either of the Cold War’s rival military blocs. The meeting placed the country in a network with states across Africa, Asia and other regions.

Economic changes in the 1960s brought both opportunities and unemployment. More Yugoslav citizens went abroad for work. Migration connected household income and family decisions with foreign labor markets, even while relatives and homes remained in the federation.

During the Second World War, the Ustaša regime operated the Jasenovac camp system in the Axis-aligned Independent State of Croatia. Serbs, Jews, Roma and political opponents were persecuted and killed there. This wartime regime must be distinguished from both the earlier Yugoslav kingdom and modern Croatia.

Serbian in Cyrillic, article 1 of the 1946 constitution: “Федеративна Народна Република Југославија је савезна народна држава републиканског облика”. Translation: “The Federal People’s Republic of Yugoslavia is a federal people’s state of republican form.” This excerpt follows the Archives of Yugoslavia’s edition of the historical text.

ending.text: The six-republic federation dissolved in 1991 and 1992 amid war and displacement. Serbia and Montenegro formed a smaller Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992, with different territory and membership. Map coverage ends in 1994, later than the federation.
